column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
Short article (about 280 words); the text uses nearly all of its substance.
The article says he conquered Fez and Sijilmasa twice (before and after 977); told once.
The entry says the post was British 'from the 1670s'; the article says English traders c. 1670. Climate, the Bush ancestry and the 2010 preservation project left out.
The entry places the room in the Castle of San Giorgio; the article says the Ducal Palace. Neither named in the text.

The entry says Phan Đình Phùng died in 1895; the article says he held Hà Tĩnh 'up till 1896' and his death ended the movement, implying 1896. No year given in the text. The article's 'catastrophe at Bình Định broke the power of the Cần Vương in northern Annam' seems a slip for Ba Đình; left out.
The article's 'US$10,000 for 26 years' is ambiguous (a yearly sum or in all); kept in its words.

The article's opening sentence calls him 'the Spanish viceroy of New Spain', an evident slip; ignored. The article says he 'inherited' the Alva Ixtlilxochitl collection on the historian's death in 1650 and also that the son gave it to him; dates left out. The entry calls him a friend of Sor Juana, which the article supports.

The article dates his time as toqui roughly 1553-1558, while the entry says he led after Lautaro's death in 1557; 1553 left out. The article gives 5 February 1558 both as the day of the attack on Cañete and as the day of his capture at Antihuala; neither date given. The entry places his execution at Cañete; the article only says he was led towards Tucapel and taken before Reinoso; no place given.
The article places Cayor in northern and central Senegal; the entry says western Senegal; location not given. The article gives an end date of 1886.

The article dates the ships' call at the Isle of Wight to October 1632, which cannot fit a charter of June 1632 and a landing in March 1634; left out. It dates the Toleration Act both 21 April and 21 September 1649; not told (the entry names it).

The article does not say how Cersobleptes ended (eliminated or subjugated, circumstances unknown); the entry says Philip defeated him in 342-341 BCE and annexed most of his lands, which the text does not contradict. The cession of the Chersonese 357 BCE is the article's date but Isocrates is less certain; left as the entry has it.
The article's chronology of Abunai's revolt (two months, then a battle on 20 April 1675) is odd; kept in its words.

The article's lead lists victories against the Liao, but its body says that against the Northern Han and the Liao 'nothing substantial came of it'; the entry says he took territory from the Liao. The Liao outcome is left out.

The entry says Hyspaosines refounded the city around 141 BCE; the article says it was rebuilt c. 166 BCE on the order of Antiochus IV, with Hyspaosines as satrap overseeing the work. Neither date nor who ordered the rebuilding is given. The article also says an Arab chieftain Spasines enlarged the town, which conflicts with the naming after Hyspaosines; left out.
The article gives the Lisbon marriage as 13 or 30 October 1791; only 'that autumn' is said.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance beyond the entry: birth, parents, regency, the 1728 inheritance and lists of children only

The article says that after the constitution of 30 December Hérard 'soon afterward' seized control and declared himself president, which conflicts with its own date of 4 April 1843 for his declaration; the text gives only the dates in order and leaves the 'seized control' sequence out. The article's casualty figures (2 Dominicans killed against 1,000 Haitians) are given as it states them.

The entry says he governed from the Mughan plain; the article names Ganja as his power base (or Ani and Kars in some sources); no seat is given. The entry says illness ended his command; the article says only that he died around 1241.

The article dates his creation as cardinal to 17 May 1706, before his election to Esztergom in 1707; the entry's wording ('in 1707 and a cardinal') can be read as both in 1707, so the cardinal's date is left out here.
SKIPPED: article of about 330 words, most of it already in the entry's description (midwives, Culhuacan, the bones of earlier ages, the skull-faced warrior figure, the official title and Tlacaelel)
The article's Black Dinner section is empty in the saved copy, so the events of 1440 are not told. The entry's 1452 and 1455 events are not in the saved text and are not repeated.
The article gives his retirement both as 'at 1976' (lead) and as 31 December 1975 (Presidency section); the entry says he served until 1975. The retirement date is left out.

The article dates its production 'around 700' and says only the León palimpsest is older as a complete one-volume Latin Bible; the entry says 'early 8th century' and 'oldest surviving complete manuscript'. Neither point is repeated.
Bemborough's nationality and first name are uncertain in the sources (Robert or Richard; English or German); the text keeps to the entry's Robert Bemborough.

The entry says the brothers founded Freiburg in 1120; the article says they granted it city rights in 1120. The text uses the article's wording without saying 'founded'. The article spells the emperor Lothar III, the entry Lothair III.

The article calls the Alphabet Prayer 'the first original poetry in Old Church Slavonic'; the entry says 'one of the earliest poems in Slavonic', so no claim of primacy is made for it here. The entry's statement that he became bishop of Preslav is not in the article.
The 'second largest global reserve of copper' figure was left out as a present-day ranking.
The entry says some 30,000 people speak Cora today; the article gives the 2000 census figures (24,390 in Cora-speaking households, 16,357 speakers). No figure is given here.
The entry dates the foundation to around 657; the article gives 661 (and its abbot list starts in 662). No foundation year is given here.

The article dates his death and the defeat to 86 and places it at Tapae (the First Battle of Tapae); the entry says 86 or 87 and 'possibly at Tapae'. Neither the year of the defeat nor the site is given here. The article also dates Galba's murder to 'January 15, 68', a slip for 69; left out.
The article says he was governor of Milan for 20 months without dates; the entry gives 1556 and 1557. Not repeated.

The article spells the emperor Gelawdewos; the entry Galawdewos. Clements Markham's claim that Gama was captured because he would not retreat without a woman he had captured is left out as a late, unsupported story.

The article says his satrapy was Cappadocia or Cilicia (the evidence is contradictory); the entry says Cappadocia. The province he inherited is left unnamed. The second Luwian form 'Tarkumuwa' in the article's Name section is a variant spelling of Tarkamuwa.
The tomb owner is spelled Djehutihotep and Djehutyhotep in the article; the entry uses Djehutyhotep.
The article's section on a ban on renting houses to non-citizens is a present-day municipal policy and is left out.
Pete Seeger's album title (Dangerous Songs!?) left out to avoid the doubled punctuation check.

Entry says he deposed Cabeza de Vaca in 1544; the article gives no year, so none is printed. Article gives death both as 3 October 1556 and 'around 1556'; text says 1556. Article gives the encomienda figure as 'between 20,000 and 17,000'.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (much of it a quoted stanza) and adds little beyond the entry

The entry says she was canonised in 1976; the article says she was beatified by Pope Paul VI in 1976. Neither outcome is printed; the text stops at the process resuming in 1955. The entry may need correcting.
Left out the 2026 Iranian propaganda video and other recent popular-culture uses.

The article says that by 452 BCE he had united central Sicily; the entry dates the league to around 460 BCE. The year of union is left out. Article gives death as 440 BCE; entry c. 440 BCE. Printed as the year he died with Diodorus' 440 date, consistent with both.
Article gives his life as 590-634; the entry gives only d. 634, so the birth year is left out.
The article's lead says he served as lieutenant governor of Guernsey for four years; the body gives 1704 to 1708, which is printed.

Death left out: the entry says he was captured and sacrificed in 1115; the article gives Charles C. Mann's version (captured and sacrificed by Four Wind at age 55, which would be about 1118) and John Pohl's (assassinated by Four Wind on a hunting trip). The article dates the conquest of Xipe's Bundle and the killing of Eleven Wind to 1101 but gives Eleven Wind's dates as 1027-1099; the year is left out. The article calls Six Lizard both his half-sister and his stepsister; half-sister used. The entry's Tututepec c. 1083 and the winning of Tilantongo are not in the article and are not repeated.

Entry dates his victory over Later Yan to Canhe Slope in 395; the article's lead speaks of defeating Murong Bao in 397. Only the capture of Zhongshan in 397 (from the article's body) is printed, which does not contradict the entry. Grandfather's name spelled Tuoba Shiyijian in the entry and Tuoba Shiyiqian in the article: left unnamed in the text.
The entry's peace with the Southern Song in 1165 is not in the article and is not repeated.

The entry dates the persecution of Buddhism from 446; the article's lead says he ordered the abolition of Buddhism in 444. The year is left out of the text. The entry's conquest of Northern Liang in 439 is not in the excerpt and is not repeated.
The Yuan Huangtou kite flight and the treatment of Consort Xue's body are left out as detail beyond what the summary needs.
The article calls him the fifth emperor of the Liu Song; the entry says fourth. No ordinal is printed. The entry's Daming calendar of Zu Chongzhi (462) is not in the article and is not repeated.

The article calls his father Shizong's second son; the Shizong article's family list makes Wanyan Yungong the first son. Neither is printed. Entry calls his reign the height of Confucian government and names the Taihe Code and the 1194 Yellow River shift, which the article does not give; not repeated. The article stresses decline under him; the text gives the facts without the article's word 'incompetency'.

The entry's taking of Arezzo in 1384 is not in the article (only '1384 Italian campaign') and is not repeated. The article says Isabella died in 1379 and that he remarried in 1386 in one garbled sentence, and gives his daughter by Isabelle of Lorraine as born on an unknown date and as 1386-1411; the second marriage is left out.

The article both says the parliament officially sat 20 March to 29 April 1850 and that 'the Erfurt parliament never materialised'; the entry says a union parliament met in spring 1850, so the text gives the opening and session dates and leaves out 'never materialised'. The Olmütz date (29 November 1850) is left to the entry, which gives November 1850.

Entry says the Treaty of Angers recognised him as king; the article argues he was probably not a king (rex) and that the royal seal was a right granted by Charles. Left the question of the title out apart from the recorded styles. Article dates his death 2 or 12 November 857; entry only 857. Wrote November 857. The article places Nominoe's death during the 849 offensive without a year; I did not give a year for it.

The article gives 28 November 1917 for the declaration of supreme authority in its lead, but its body has the proclamation at the last meeting on 15 November and forcible dissolution on 26 November (Old and New Style mixed). The entry says 28 November. Left all these days out. The entry says the assembly first met in July 1917; the article gives no first meeting date but says the town deputies were elected in July and August.

The article dates the war 1529–1543 (the conventional start, Shimbra Kure) but also records a raid in 1527; the entry gives 1527–1543. I did not state a start year for the war, only the dated clashes. Accounts differ on who fired the shot that wounded Ahmad (João de Castilho or Pero de Lião); left unnamed.

The entry dates Porus' murder around 317 BCE; the article says only that it happened after Alexander's death in 323 BCE (Diodorus). I kept the article's 'after 323' wording without a year for the murder itself. The article calls the battle 'the first Battle of Gabiene' (usually called Paraitakene); I wrote 'the first great battle with Antigonus' to avoid the doubtful name.
The article is short on political history (nothing on Matsumae or the shogunate, which the entry covers); the text keeps to the divisions, the name and its Western description.

The article gives two dates for his creation as cardinal: 2 September 1791 and 21 February 1794 (cardinal deacon of Sant'Angelo in Pescheria). I left the year out. The article's account of his years 1800-1814 is confused (lived quietly in Naples under Joseph and Murat; also ambassador to Paris for Ferdinand); kept to the dated facts.

The entry says that after 1814 he lived quietly in Bologna; the article says he retired with Elisa to Trieste and moved to Bologna only after her death in 1820. Left the place of his retirement before 1820 out. The entry says he was military commander in Tuscany from 1809; the article has 'governor of Poscane in 1809' (apparently a slip). Left out.
The article gives his birth year as 1805; the entry's dates are 1806–1836. Birth year left out. The article dates his death 18 February in the lead and 19 February in the text; no day given.
The article is short (about 300 words); the text uses nearly all of it.

The article says the town was recaptured 'at the Battle of Sattelberg' on 2 October 1943; Sattelberg was a later battle, so I named only the Huon Peninsula campaign. The airport 'has no scheduled air service as of 2023': left out under the no 'as of' rule.
The traditional presence of Teutonic Knights and Hospitallers at Legnica is called a later addition in the article; only the Templars are mentioned.

The article says the site was first, accidentally, found in 1805 (a pavement and column fragments), and rediscovered in 1960; the entry says 'discovered in 1960'. Left 1805 out. Miles Russell re-dates the palace to the early 90s CE, against the entry's c. 75: left his date out and mentioned the Lucullus theory without it. The article calls it the largest Roman residence north of the Alps; the entry says in Britain. Not repeated.

The entry says both sides shared command; the article says Dionysius' version omits any joint command, and that a fragment of L. Cincius may imply alternating command, which probably never happened. Left the question of command out. The article's lead dates the treaty to 493 BC; not repeated, as the entry gives c. 493 BCE.
The article says the fort outlines are laid in granite slabs (lead) and in brick (body); wrote only that they are marked.
The article dates his birth c. 1382; the entry c. 1380. Birth year and his age when Visconti hired him ('in his thirtieth year') left out.

The article's lead says he was re-elected president in 1895; its body gives the re-election as 22 November 1893. No year given for the re-election (not mentioned). The lead says he won the 1888 election unopposed; the body says a landslide victory. Not mentioned.
The article calls Pompeius 'Quintus Pompeius' as proconsul of 140 and 'Pompeius, the former consul of 141'; I used Quintus Pompeius without a year.
The article lists Gandhari on coins and as Kushan official language; no conflict with the entry's dates.

The article dates Heraclius's sack of Ganzak to 622; the entry says 624. The year is left out of the text. The article gives Leylan as the site according to Minorsky, Schippmann and Boyce; the entry says the site is still debated. The text attributes the identification to those scholars. The article says Adur Gushnasp was built under the Atropatenian kingdom; it does not mention Takht-e Soleyman. Not repeated. Two sections only: the article is short (about 400 words).
The entry names Old Phocaea among the family's lands; the article does not mention it. Not repeated.

SKIPPED: the article has about 300 words, nearly all of which the entry already gives (Han'e, low standing, Tang and Song songs, Ming cultivation, Qing ban); only an idiom, Xu Yuan and Xue Susu would be new
The article does not date the proclamation of the Autonomous Republic of Cochinchina; the entry's June 1946 is not repeated or contradicted.
The article says Templer was High Commissioner from 22 January 1952; it does not give the end date, which the entry has as 1954.

The article gives his death as probably 877, certainly before 879; the entry has c. 878. No year is given in the text. The article does not mention the Viking raids on the Rhône that the entry names. The article's sequence is odd: Bertha defends Vienne in 870 though Girart administered Provence until 869; kept as given.
The article calls Niels Ebbesen a Danish squire; the entry a Jutish nobleman. Neither label is used beyond his name.
Short article (about 300 words); two sections. Josephus's role as the source is in the entry and the article.
SKIPPED: the article has about 300 words of substance; a text from it came to 208 words. It also says the process was patented in 1877, where the entry dates it to 1879
SKIPPED: article of about 260 words, most of it already in the entry; it also dates his rule from 591 and the Avar invasion and his death to 611 (probably), where the entry has c. 590 and 610

The article dates the fortification to early Late Helladic III B, c. 1300 BC; the entry says built in the 13th century BCE. No date is given in the text. The article does not give the abandonment around 1200 BCE that the entry names.
The article's text names the generals 'Wu and Yuwen' in one passage and Yu Zhongwen elsewhere; only Yu Zhongwen and Yuwen Shu are used.
SKIPPED: the article has about 120 words of history (16th-century Jat settlement, Bhim Singh Rana, Chhatar Singh Rana); the rest is census, climate and transport figures
The article does not mention the right to invest bishops that the entry names; not repeated.

The article dates Alvarado's attack on Cicumba's camp to late May or early June 1536 in one place and Cereceda's letter places the battle in late June 1536; written as 1536 only. Oviedo reported Guerrero dead by 1532, left out. Hernández de Córdoba's first name is not in the file.
The article spells the minaret's builder Yaghmorasan and calls him founder of the Abdalwadid dynasty; the entry spells him Yaghmurasen. He is not named in the text to avoid two spellings on one page.
The article dates Weltgeschichte to 1860 in the text and to 1856–59 (6 vols.) in the works list; no date given.
The Later Baekje king is spelt Kyŏn Hwŏn in the article and Gyeon Hwon in the entry; not named in the text. The family list spells the princess Nakrang, the text Nangrang.

The article gives no founding date and no date for the move to Dhrangadhra; the entry's late 15th century and 18th century are not repeated. Rankings (cotton, market yard) and literacy comparisons left out.
The article is short; everything in the text is from it.

The article gives the Mahavamsa dates 544–413 BCE and a later scholarly chronology (Sarao: Bimbisara c. 457–405 BCE, Udayin c. 373–357 BCE, i.e. 5th to 4th century BCE), which differs from the entry's 6th–5th century BCE; no dates printed. Ajatashatru's reign is given as 493–462 BCE in the text and 492–460 BCE in the list. Jain texts have Nanda succeed the childless Udayin, against the entry's Shishunaga; that succession is left out.
The article gives the founding of ALOHA as 1969 (Budnick) or 1972 (Maxwell); not used.

The article contradicts itself on the inquiry: one passage says it found he had taken more than five million talers of public money, another that his fortune came from the king's prodigality rather than unlawful means. Neither is printed.

The article dates Cunningham's discovery to 1877 in the text but heads the section 'Survey by Alexander Cunningham in 1874–1875'; no year printed. Edwin Bryant is cited for Heliodorus's conversion 'in the first century BCE', against the entry's c. 113 BCE; left out. The king is spelt Antialkidas in the article, Antialcidas in the entry.

The article gives his birth as c. 1504 and his death as c. 1578 (later simply 1578); the entry has c. 1501. Birth year not printed. The letter's addressee is spelt 'Santo Domino' in the article; not named.
The article gives Malhar Rao Holkar I's birth as 1694 in the text and 16 March 1693 in the list, and Marthand Rao's accession as 17 January 1834 in the text and 1833 in the list; neither is printed.

The article spells the rival president Jiménez in one passage and Jimenes elsewhere; the 1902 coup sentence names no one. The article dates the Heureaux conspiracy to 1889; date not printed since Heureaux was murdered in 1899.
The article places the Istrian lands in northern Dalmatia in its lead; not repeated.
The article calls the 1630 rank 'imperial counts (Reichsfreiherren)'; left out. It names the Prussian buyer of 1791 as Friedrich Wilhelm II; written as Prussia.

SKIPPED: The article has too little history (a few lines on its Sui to Ming administration) and says nothing of Huatai, Zhai Wei or Southern Yan; the rest is lists of subdivisions and a modern court case.

The article dates occupation to the 1st to 9th century AD and has platforms rebuilt every 100 years 'during six centuries'; the entry gives c. 100–800 CE. No span printed. The article names the capital Cerro Blanco, the entry Huacas de Moche; the capital is not named.
The article is short; the Five-Year Plan proposal in its lead is left out.

The article calls Baldwin II Hugh's cousin and Melisende his second cousin; the entry says cousin of Melisende. Left the relationship out. Birth year: Mayer dates it 1106-1110; the entry gives c. 1106. Not stated.

The entry says defeat at Kinsale in 1601 forced his submission; the article gives the surrender to Mountjoy in 1603 at Mellifont. Left the date of submission out. Died 10 July (Old Style), 20 July (New Style) 1616: written as July 1616.

The article says Huhanye was defeated by Zhizhi in 51 BC and then submitted; the entry gives submission in 51 BCE. Consistent, year not repeated. The article's lead names his successor as Diaotaomogao, the family list as Fuzhulei Ruodi (r. 31-20 BC). Wrote neither as the first successor by name order beyond 'in turn'. The entry calls him chanyu of the Southern Xiongnu; the article only says Xiongnu.

The article gives his death as August 1057, 'or 1056 according to some sources'; the entry gives 1057. Not dated in the text. The entry gives c. 1010 as birth and 1051 as the start of his rule; the article gives neither.

The entry's ox-hide story of Elissa/Dido is not in the article; not repeated or contradicted. Silius Italicus' Hiarbas is called a Gaetulian leader in one place and Garamante in another in the article; left his people out.

Reign dates in the article: c. 1490-1465 BC or around 1450 BC; the entry says 15th century BCE. No reign dates given. The article names his son as Niqmepa in most places but the inscription quotation names Adad-niari as the son he entrusted things to; used Niqmepa only for the seal, as the article does.
SKIPPED: article has under about 250 words of substance: hydrology, a deity festival, two lines of colonial history and present-day pollution; nothing on the palm-oil trade or Opobo

The entry says the PNI was founded on 4 July 1927; the article says the study club became the Indonesian National Association on 4 July 1927 and took the name Indonesian National Party in May 1928. Wrote 'July 1927' for the Association and May 1928 for the name, which does not contradict the founding date. The entry counts the post-independence PNI among the four largest parties in 1955; the article says it came first.

The entry places the monastery at Kostroma on the Volga; the article says on the bank of the Kostroma River opposite the city. Left its setting out. The article says Karamzin found three 14th-century chronicles there, the Hypatian Codex; the entry mentions the codex. Not repeated. The 1275 founder is given in the article only as Yaroslavich.
The entry says Karim Khan ruled as regent (vakil); the article gives the title Vakil-e daulat to Ali Mardan in 1750. Wrote 'at first' for Ali Mardan so the two do not clash.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little to the entry

The entry places his final defeat at Qasr al-Jiss; the article says the defeat was at Samarra. Left the place out. The entry dates Sabuktakin's mutiny to 974; the article gives no year for it. Not dated. The entry gives birth 943; the article gives none.

The entry says he surrendered Alexandria in September 1801; the article gives the surrender on 30 August 1801. Left the date out. The article places the March 1801 defeat at 'La Muiron', a name that does not fit a landing site; the entry says near Alexandria. Left out.
The article gives his death as 12 June 1828 in the lead and 11 June 1828 in the text; written as June 1828.

SKIPPED: the lead adds little beyond the entry, and the two further sections (a 1268 Mongol war with 300,000 men and 100,000 elephants; Prey Nokor, tribute in 1285) are unsourced in tone and contradict the lead, which has the tribute in 1283

The article gives his governorship as 1691-1700 in the lead and 1691-1703 in a later section; the entry gives 1691-1700. No end date written. The article says he was 'actually born in Pau', not Saubusse; the entry gives 1646 only, so the place does not contradict it. The entry says the 1689 Suriname attack failed; the article gives no outcome. Not mentioned.

The article says New Orleans became the capital 'by 1723' and that the move was completed in August 1722; the entry says 1722. Used the 1722 move only. Baptised 23 February 1680; exact birth day unknown, so written as early 1680.

The article says she recruited the three sisters in 1657 and later refers to 'the three nuns whom she had recruited in 1659'; used 1657 for the journey and October 1659 for their arrival, as the article's main narrative does.

The article says in its lead that he and his brother Yakchŏn were baptized in 1874 (an evident slip) and later that there is no proof he was ever baptized: his own faith is left out. The article's tea-revival section (he taught monks to make caked tea) was left out for length.
The 1128/29 CE date is given as in the article (1186 VS).
The article says the Jin envoys came for Zhang Jue in 1123 or 1124 (records differ); only the defection year 1123 is given.
Short article (about 480 words); the text uses nearly all of it.
The article spells the county sold to Brandenburg in 1681 both Rosenburg and Rosenberg; that sale is left out.
The article's lead dates the sentence of death to 1694; the body places the second petition three years after 1689. No year is given for the sentence.
The article gives the family's move to Saint Petersburg as 1910 in its lead and 1907 in its body: no year is printed. His son, a physicist who may be living, is left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words, much of it already in the description; not enough for 260 words without padding

The article gives his governorship as 1598-1610 and his exile as 1614 in places, against the recall of 1606 told in its Later life section; no end year of the governorship is printed. The entry dates his birth c. 1550; the article says 1550: no birth year is printed.
The entry says he was elected in October 1931; the article gives no election month, only that he took office on 15 November.
The lists of present jurisdictions and the Jamaican reform debate are left out; the article's present-tense lists are not reproduced.

The entry calls her an Augustinian nun; the article calls her a Norbertine canoness who restored strict Augustinian rules as prioress. Her order is not named in the text. The article dates the bishop's death 1246 in one place and 1247 in another; no year is printed for Roger's return.

The entry says he discovered the Paracas cemeteries in 1925; the article says he first visited the site in 1925 and found the bundles in 1927. Both dates are given as the article frames them, without saying when the cemeteries were discovered.
The entry says the founders came from Amsterdam and that some went on to New Amsterdam; the article says neither, and neither is repeated or contradicted.
The entry says its leaders had fled to Vietnam; the article places the founding group inside Cambodia around Kratie and does not mention flight to Vietnam. Neither is stated.
The entry calls him a conservative ruler; the article says nothing of his politics.
The entry dates Ibn Karram's death to 869; the article gives 896. No year is printed. The article calls the sect Hanafi-Mujassim-Murji'ah; the entry calls it Sunni. The label is left out.

The article dates the Mahavamsa to the 6th century AD in one section and the 5th century CE in another; no century is printed. Legend dates the Kiri Vehera to King Mahasena in the 6th century BC; only the archaeological dating is given.
The entry dates his Sumatran expedition around 1275; the article dates the Pamalayu expedition around 1290 and uses 1275 only for the term Dvipantara. No date is printed for the expedition.
Short article (about 300 words); written in two sections.

The article contradicts itself on his death: its lead gives 21 August 1941; its Death section says he was allegedly executed in 1938, or held until summer 1943 and executed on Chiang Kai-shek's orders. The entry says executed in 1941. No date of death given in the text. The article says he fell back to Kashgar on 13 January 1934 and assumed the presidency there; the entry says he never governed from Kashgar. The Kashgar arrival is left out. Year of birth (1889 in the article, c. 1889 in the entry) left out.

Amir Khusrau's dates (murder of Mubarak Shah 9 July 1320, Tughluq's accession 6 September 1320) give a reign of under two months; Isami gives two or three months. The entry's 'about two months' is kept by not stating a length. Barani's account of the sexual relationship is told only in general terms.

The article says Humbert landed at nearby Kilcummin harbour; the entry says the French landed at Killala. The landing place is left out ('seized Killala'). The article gives the round tower as 52 metres (170 feet) high, which looks wrong; left out.
Short article; the entry's strikes against labour conscription are not in it.
The article says the work was intended for the education of King Magnus Lagabøte, son of King Håkon Håkonsson; the entry says probably for the sons of King Haakon IV. The intended pupil is left out.

The article dates the Cistercian takeover to 1289 (Bolko I gave the lands to the Cistercians, who consecrated the church in 1292; 'from 1289 to 1810 run by Cistercians'); the entry says refounded for Cistercians in 1292. The year 1289 is left out.

The article says that though never a ruler he wielded much power; the entry says he took control of Larsa and installed his son. 'Never a ruler' is left out. The article calls the region Emutbal; the entry Yamutbal. Both forms occur in the article's inscription quotation.

The article mixes calendars for the Sekigahara campaign (August 21 and 22, September 14, then October 21 for the battle); day dates left out. It dates the Ki Shigefusa killing to 20 April 1588; given as 1588 only. The article places the Nadegiri 'during the first Korean campaign', while Jeolla fighting and Jiksan belong to 1597; told without assigning a campaign.
